podcast.body: Released in 1958, this instrumental was highly influential for its tone and style. Link Wray achieved new sounds through experimentation with tunings, amplifiers, distortion, and tremolo. It was banned by numerous radio stations for sounding "too dangerous" and potentially inciting violence, and it prefigured the sound of surf music. "Not only would this instrumental become very influential in terms of tone and style, but it was also banned by a bunch of radio stations because it sounded too dangerous and might incite listeners to violence."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This instrumental piece, released in 1958, lacked lyrics or an explicit message, instead featuring a slow, dirty, and raw guitar sound. It utilized a distortion that was unprecedented in its aggression on commercial radio at the time. Its title, "Rumble," referred to street gang fights, a piece of youth slang from the 1950s, which was controversial in a musical landscape dominated by doo-wop and clean ballads, becoming an anomaly that anticipated a part of rock and roll. "Su título, Rumble, hacía referencia a las peleas entre mandas callejeras, la jerga juvenil de los años 50."

podcast.body: This instrumental track by Link Wray, released in 1958, was created by intentionally poking holes in the speaker cones of his amplifier to achieve a raspy, distorted sound. The song was so controversial for its time that it was banned by some radio stations, who feared it encouraged juvenile delinquency and gang fights. Its unique sound proved hugely influential, inspiring guitarists globally to seek ways to duplicate it. "This song was so sinister for its day that it was banned by some radio stations believing that it encouraged not just juvenile delinquency, but gangfights."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This was Link Wray's first single, released in 1958, and was a fuzzy, distorted instrumental, highly unique for its era, predating fuzz pedals. Wray achieved its "dirty and dangerous sound" by poking holes in his amplifier's speaker, after initially experimenting with a composition titled "Oddball." "In 1958, he released his first single, which was a fuzzy, distorted instrumental, very unique for its day because it was recorded years before there was such a thing as a fuzz pedal for the guitar."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
